content.text: > `codex plugin marketplace add garrytan/gbrain@codex-plugin` + `codex plugin add gbrain@gbrain` > (Claude Code: `/plugin marketplace add garrytan/gbrain` + `/plugin install gbrain@gbrain`). Default path (Bun 1.4.4 or newer is required — gbrain is a Bun + TypeScript runtime; on an older Bun, run `bun upgrade` first): ```bash curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH" bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable ``` Verify: `gbrain --version` should print a version number. If `gbrain` is not found, restart the shell or add the PATH export to the shell profile. Bun's installer needs `unzip` and stops with `error: unzip is required to install bun` without it. Check with `command -v unzip`; if it prints nothing, install it first: `apt-get update && apt-get install -y unzip` (Debian, Ubuntu), `dnf install -y unzip` (Fedora, RHEL) or `apk add unzip` (Alpine), with `sudo` in front unless you are root. No way to install packages? Use the [no-unzip route](#no-unzip), not an improvised one. **No `unzip` and no way to install packages (Linux).** This route puts the same Bun build the official installer would fetch, taken from Bun's own npm package `@oven/bun-linux-`, into `~/.bun/bin`, the directory the official installer uses, and adds that directory to the PATH of every new login shell. It needs only `curl` and `tar`: ```bash arch=$(uname -m); [ "$arch" = x86_64 ] && arch=x64; [ "$arch" = arm64 ] && arch=aarch64 mkdir -p ~/.bun/bin curl -fsSL "https://registry.npmjs.org/@oven/bun-linux-$arch/-/bun-linux-$arch-1.4.4.tgz" | tar -xzO package/bin/bun > ~/.bun/bin/bun.new && chmod +x ~/.bun/bin/bun.new && ~/.bun/bin/bun.new --version && mv ~/.bun/bin/bun.new ~/.bun/bin/bun echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.profile export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH" bun install -g github:garrytan/gbrain#stable bash -lc 'gbrain --version' ``` The PATH line goes in `~/.profile`, which new login shells read. Bash skips `~/.profile` when `~/.bash_profile` or `~/.bash_login` exists, so append the line to that file instead; zsh reads `~/.zprofile`. On Alpine or another musl system, run `arch=$arch-musl` after the first line; on an x64 CPU without AVX2, run `arch=x64-baseline`. The last command must print a version from a fresh shell. Don't install Bun with `npm install -g bun` or run gbrain from a git clone instead: gbrain starts with `#!/usr/bin/env bun`, so it fails in any new shell that can't find `bun` on its PATH. Next, on Claude Code or Codex: `gbrain setup claude-code` (or `gbrain setup codex`), which needs no API key ([Step 3](#step-3-create-the-brain)). On any other harness, `gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding` (Step 3). **A command scanner blocks the Bun installer or `bun install` (Hermes).** Some harnesses check each shell command before running it and refuse what they can't approve without a person. Hermes in single-query mode refuses `curl … | bash`, `bun install -g github:…` (its scanner, Tirith, can't finish a package lookup for a `github:` spec) and commands that append to a dotfile such as `~/.profile`. Install the release binary instead: one file built from the same release, which needs no Bun, no git and no package install. Run each line as its own command, exactly as written (Linux x64; on an Apple Silicon Mac use `gbrain-darwin-arm64`): ```bash curl -fL --create-dirs -o ~/.local/bin/gbrain https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/releases/latest/download/gbrain-linux-x64 chmod +x ~/.local/bin/gbrain ~/.local/bin/gbrain --version ~/.local/bin/gbrain init --pglite --no-embedding ``` `releases/latest` is the stable release. Use the absolute path `~/.local/bin/gbrain` in every command and MCP registration instead of editing shell profiles. Run each line as written: an added `2>&1`, `$(…)` or `{ …; }` group can make the scanner refuse a line it would otherwise pass. Then run `~/.local/bin/gbrain setup hermes`: it registers gbrain through Hermes's own `hermes mcp add` (no hand edit of Hermes's protected `config.yaml`), adds the brain-first rule and its per-turn hook, and checks the server with `hermes mcp test gbrain`. If it prints a `hermes mcp add` command instead, or (an older gbrain) says setup does not register Hermes's MCP server, run the registration command from [docs/mcp/HERMES.md](docs/mcp/HERMES.md#register-by-hand) with `~/.local/bin/gbrain` as the command. If the user would rather keep the Bun install, Hermes's own refusal names its setting for this: `approvals.single_query_mode: approve` in Hermes's config, which is the user's call. `gbrain upgrade` updates a release binary in place. > **If `bun install -g` aborts or `gbrain doctor` reports `schema_version: 0`** > ([#218](https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/issues/218)), run `gbrain apply-migrations --yes --no-autopilot-install`. > Exit 0 means the schema is at head. Exit 1 with `migrations_pending` means it is still behind and another > `--yes` repeats the failure: run `gbrain doctor --json`, tell the user what it reports, and use the > deterministic install below. Reason `wedged` means one migration failed three or more times in a row: > relay its `fix`; the user fixes the cause and runs `gbrain apply-migrations --force-retry ` > (reinstalling does not help). > > ```bash > git clone --branch stable https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain.git ~/gbrain && cd ~/gbrain > bun install && bun link > ``` ## Step 2: API Keys Configured cloud providers receive text: embedding inputs, queries and candidate passages for reranking, and source or retrieved content for LLM extraction and synthesis. The harness's own model receives the memory it recalls even when GBrain is keyless. Explain these boundaries before enabling a capability; see [memory boundaries](docs/guides/memory-boundaries.md#where-text-goes). Skip API-key setup for the initial keyless memory path. gbrain skillpack scaffold <name> | <source> | --all [--workspace PATH] [--dry-run] [--trust] [--no-cache] [--json]

<name>   — bundled skill slug (e.g. `book-mirror`)
<source> — third-party skillpack source. Accepted shapes:
             owner/repo                (expands to https://github.com/owner/repo)
             https://...git            (verbatim https URL)
             ./local/dir/              (local pack root)
             ./local/pack.tgz          (local tarball)

Flags:
  --workspace PATH    Target workspace (default: auto-detected)
  --all               Scaffold every bundled skill (gbrain only)
  --dry-run           Validate + report; no writes
  --trust             The user's approval to trust a new third-party author + pin
                      (without it a non-interactive run writes nothing and exits 3)
  --no-cache          Force fresh clone/extract for third-party sources
  --json              Stable JSON envelope for agent consumption
gbrain init — initialize a brain (PGLite or Supabase Postgres)

USAGE
  gbrain init [flags]

ENGINE SELECTION (mutually exclusive)
  --pglite              Use embedded PGLite (zero-config, the default)
  --supabase            Use Supabase Postgres (recommended for 1000+ files)
  --url <URL>           Use a manual Postgres connection string
  --mcp-only            Thin-client mode: connect to a remote gbrain MCP, no local engine

OPTIONS
  --force               Overwrite an existing config (gated by default)
  --non-interactive     Don't prompt; use defaults
  --migrate-only        Apply pending schema migrations against the configured engine
                        without re-saving config (used by post-upgrade and orchestrators)
  --json                JSON output for status reporting
  --content-root <path> Use a new owned content directory (existing source roots win)
  --db-only             Keep memory database-only; shared publication needs export/adoption
  --git                 Authorize Git init in the new owned empty content directory
  --no-git              Keep a content directory without Git (default)
  --path <DIR>          Override default brain path (PGLite only)
  --key <APIKEY>        Provide an API key non-interactively (Supabase only)
  --embedding-model <PROVIDER:MODEL>
                        e.g. openai:text-embedding-3-large, voyage:voyage-multimodal-3
  --model <PROVIDER>    Shorthand: pick recipe default for a provider
  --embedding-dimensions <N>
                        Embedding dimensions (must match the model)
  --expansion-model <PROVIDER:MODEL>
                        Model for query expansion (default: anthropic:claude-haiku)
  --chat-model <PROVIDER:MODEL>
                        Default subagent driver (v0.27+)
  --no-embedding        Defer embedding setup (skips the embedding-key check)
  --surface <verbs|starter|full>  Tool surface the printed harness registration pins, listed in full
                                  (default: starter, listing the memory verbs and request_tools)
  --search-mode <conservative|balanced|tokenmax>  Record the operator's search mode (no first-run ask; an existing brain's mode needs --force)
  --skip-embed-check    Skip the init-time embedding-key validation (config +
                        live test-embed). Also via GBRAIN_INIT_SKIP_EMBED_CHECK=1

EXAMPLES
  gbrain init --pglite                      # Local-only, no API keys
  gbrain init --supabase                    # Interactive Supabase setup
  gbrain init --url postgresql://...        # Use a custom Postgres
  gbrain init --mcp-only --issuer-url https://host:3001 --mcp-url https://host:3001/mcp --oauth-client-id <id> --oauth-client-secret <secret>  # Thin-client mode

NOTES
  - Bare `gbrain init` always defaults to PGLite at ~/.gbrain/brain.pglite.
    In a directory with 1000+ .md files it prints a suggestion to use
    `gbrain init --supabase` (faster search at scale) but still proceeds
    with PGLite.
  - Existing config is preserved unless --force is passed.

# Connect GBrain to OpenClaw

> This page is the MCP-registration reference card. For the full brain install
> — CLI, engine, skills, dream cycle — follow
> [INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md](../../INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md); the README covers the
> bootstrap and connect paths.

Connect with [Option 2](#option-2-openclaw-mcp-add) (stdio) when the brain runs on
the gateway's machine, or with
[OpenClaw's own MCP client](#remote-brain-openclaws-mcp-client-over-https) when it
runs elsewhere. Option 1's ClawHub bundle is not available yet.
A bot that several people DM connects over HTTP as well: see
[One bot for several people, in DMs](#one-bot-for-several-people-in-dms).

## Option 1: ClawHub bundle plugin (not available yet)

This project publishes no ClawHub package yet. The package named `gbrain` on
ClawHub is an unofficial upload of an old 0.10.1 build whose manifest has no
`id`, so `openclaw plugins install clawhub:gbrain` stops with
`plugin manifest requires id`. Don't install it; use Option 2.

GBrain ships [`openclaw.plugin.json`](../../openclaw.plugin.json) at the repo
root. Installing the bundle plugin registers the MCP server for you — the
manifest carries an `mcpServers.gbrain` entry that runs the bundled
`.agents/gbrain-launcher serve` (the same launcher the Codex and Claude Code
plugins use; it resolves your installed `gbrain` via `GBRAIN_BIN`, then
`~/.bun/bin/gbrain`, then `PATH`, so it works under launchd's bare PATH and
never needs a build step) plus the bundled skills — and declares the
`gbrain-context-engine` context engine. To route OpenClaw's context-engine slot
through gbrain, two steps, in this order:

1. Install and enable the plugin by its own id, `gbrain-context-engine`
   (the `id` in `openclaw.plugin.json`).
2. Set the slot to the engine id the plugin registers:

   ```
   plugins.slots.contextEngine = gbrain-context-engine
   ```

The current host requires the canonical plugin ID in the slot. The installed
plugin ID is unchanged and `gbrain-context` remains a registry alias for older
integrations, but it is not a slot alias on current hosts: migrate an old
`plugins.slots.contextEngine = gbrain-context` setting to
`gbrain-context-engine`. Setting the slot alone does not install/enable the
plugin. For a legacy host that cannot provide a per-session workspace, set
`plugins.entries.gbrain-context-engine.config.workspaceDir` to an absolute
workspace path; on multi-agent hosts prefer the host-supplied workspace. An
unbound or ambiguous workspace warns and reads no source rather than selecting
an arbitrary agent's memory.

The factory also accepts zero arguments from current hosts. Its `assemble`
keeps the current prompt separate from fenced stored transcript history; an
identical trailing legacy user message is already the current turn. The
admitted-turn acknowledgement is stateless and writes nothing. Reflex-only
pointer synthesis leaves returned messages unchanged; the turn acknowledgement
does not automatically capture conversation content (compaction has its own
explicit checkpoint path). Loading the plugin alone is not evidence of model
recall: verify saved-page retrieval after a restarted turn and source isolation
with the intended host. The loopback native test uses a deterministic provider,
so it does not certify paid-model recall or provenance.

## Option 2: `openclaw mcp add`

OpenClaw keeps MCP servers under `mcp.servers` in `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`
(`openclaw config schema` shows the key path). Register gbrain with the CLI,
then run `gbrain setup openclaw` so a new session knows to use it:

```bash
openclaw mcp add gbrain --command "$(command -v gbrain)" --arg serve --arg --surface --arg starter --arg --advertise --arg verbs --env GBRAIN_HOME=$HOME
gbrain setup openclaw
```

The second line is not optional. Without it the tools are registered but
nothing tells the agent to use them, and a new session answers from OpenClaw's
own memory and chat history instead (in the [install eval](https://github.com/garrytan/harness-evals/blob/master/docs/benchmarks/2026-11-17-gbrain-install/results/README.md),
11 of the 30 OpenClaw runs without gbrain's install block missed this way).
See [Brain-first instructions](#brain-first-instructions).

Use an absolute `--command` path: the launchd-started gateway's `PATH` does
not include `~/.bun/bin`, so a bare `gbrain` fails to spawn. `--env` is
optional: a PGLite brain needs no `DATABASE_URL`
(`--env DATABASE_URL=postgresql://...` for Postgres), and `GBRAIN_HOME` only
matters when the brain home isn't `~/.gbrain`. `--surface starter --advertise verbs`
lists the seven-verb memory protocol ([MEMORY_VERBS v1](../protocol/MEMORY_VERBS_v1.md))
plus `request_tools`, which reaches every other tool; drop the
`--advertise verbs` values to list the starter set (`full` for the whole catalog) (check
`openclaw mcp add --help` for your version's `--arg` spelling).

Leave `GBRAIN_SOURCE` unset in the MCP env unless you deliberately want
single-source retrieval: a pin scopes every tool (search, `get_brain_identity`
counts, …) to that one source, and nothing warns on reads.

## Remote brain: OpenClaw's MCP client over HTTPS

When the brain runs on another machine, OpenClaw connects to its MCP endpoint
itself, over streamable HTTP with OAuth. That grant is scoped and revocable on
the brain host, while the stdio route above gives the gateway full local
database access.

```bash
openclaw gateway stop
openclaw mcp add gbrain --url https://<brain-host>/mcp --transport streamable-http --auth oauth
openclaw mcp login gbrain
openclaw mcp doctor gbrain --probe
openclaw gateway start
```

`mcp add`, `login` and `doctor --probe` refuse while the local gateway runs, so
stop it first and start it again after. `openclaw mcp login` runs the browser sign-in (on a headless host it prints a
`--code` command to finish with). OpenClaw registers its client through dynamic
client registration, so the brain owner turns that on and approves the consent
([native OAuth path](../guides/hosted-harness-access.md#native-oauth-path),
[self-service registration](ADMIN.md#self-service-dynamic-registration)). Until
the login succeeds, OpenClaw leaves the server out of agent turns. Publish the
endpoint with `gbrain mcp expose` ([remote MCP](../guides/remote-mcp.md)).

### Or: a thin client's stdio bridge

When OpenClaw should keep a stdio entry, install gbrain on the OpenClaw
machine as a thin client of the brain host and register its `gbrain serve`,
which relays every call to the host with that client's grant (it opens no
local database). On the brain host, `gbrain agent register` with
`--harness openclaw` prints these lines with your client filled in; run them
on the OpenClaw machine:

```bash
gbrain init --mcp-only --issuer-url https://<brain-host> --mcp-url https://<brain-host>/mcp \
  --oauth-client-id <client_id> --oauth-client-secret <client_secret>
openclaw mcp add gbrain --command "$(command -v gbrain)" --arg serve --arg --surface --arg starter --arg --advertise --arg verbs
```

If gbrain's bundle plugin is installed there, it already registers gbrain:
run only the `init` line. To keep this client apart from another gbrain on
that machine, put `GBRAIN_HOME=<dir>` before the `init` line and add
`--env GBRAIN_HOME=<dir>` to the `mcp add` line. What the bridge relays and
how it reports failures: [stdio bridge](../architecture/thin-client.md#stdio-bridge).

## One bot for several people, in DMs

When one OpenClaw bot answers several people, each in their own DM, each DM can
read only the pages that person may read. The bot speaks to the brain as a
[shared agent](../tutorials/company-brain.md#two-scoping-models-pick-the-one-that-matches-your-shape):
every call carries an `X-Gbrain-On-Behalf-Of` header naming the person, and the
brain answers with that person's view, within the bot's own source grant. On
OpenClaw a small plugin sets the header from the DM's sender through the
[requester-scoped MCP connection resolver](https://docs.openclaw.ai/plugins/sdk-overview/infrastructure)
(`api.registerMcpServerConnectionResolver`). OpenClaw supplies the sender, not
the model, and the header rides on the transport; an audience put in tool
arguments is refused (`on_behalf_of_in_arguments`).

**Say to your agent:** *"Set up my OpenClaw bot so each DM reads only what that
person may read"*, then *"Show what alice-example's DMs can read"* (it runs
`gbrain access check --token *** --as alice-example` on the brain host).

**DMs only.** The resolver learns who sent the turn (`requesterSenderId`, with
`messageChannel` and `agentAccountId`), not whether the turn came from a group
or who else is in it. On a group turn the sender's view would be shown to the
whole group. Use this recipe only on a gateway where every conversation has one
person in it: set [`groupPolicy: "disabled"`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/groups)
on each channel and turn `dm.groupEnabled` off on Discord and Slack. Group
audiences are tracked in #8534.

### Before you share a personal brain through the bot

Each DM reads as one member, so anything that relaxes privacy for a single
member relaxes it for every person the bot serves:

- **No private-pages grant on the bot.** Never give its token
  `--private-pages granted-sources`. With it, every mapped person reads every
  `visibility: private` page in the bot's sources, which on a personal brain are
  your own private pages.
- **No private-facts grant on the bot.** Leave its token at
  `--private-facts none`. A DM call that names a person never uses that grant
  (an asserted audience reads world-only facts), so it adds nothing for the
  people the bot serves, and any call that reaches the brain without the header
  would read every fact saved private in the bot's sources.
- **Host hatches off.** `GBRAIN_REMOTE_PRIVATE_PAGES` and
  `search.remote_private_pages` apply to every remote caller on the host, this
  bot included. Leave both unset while the bot runs.
- **A dedicated token bound to no member.** Make a new token for the bot. Don't
  reuse your own agent's token or bind the bot's token to your member: your DMs
  through the bot then read like anyone else's, and your own agent keeps your
  full view.
- **Pages only you should read name you as their reader.** Today `access:
  private` and `visibility: private` hide a page from this bot. Clearing those
  labels, by hand or in bulk with `gbrain repair private-labels`, makes the
  pages readable in every DM and by `guest`. Before you clear them, give the
  pages you want to keep to yourself `readable_by: [<your member>]` or a folder
  rule (`gbrain access rule add --prefix <folder>/ --readers <your member>`).

`gbrain access check --token *** --as <member>` must show
`Private pages: none` for the bot.

### Keep the gateway's people apart too

The header separates the brain's answers. The rest of the gateway has to keep
people apart as well
([OpenClaw's trust model](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security/trust-model)
treats one gateway as one trust boundary, so people who must not trust each
other need separate gateways):

- [`session.dmScope: "per-channel-peer"`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/session)
  (`per-account-channel-peer` with several accounts on one channel). The default,
  `main`, puts every DM in one session, so one person's brain results land in
  the next person's context.
- `tools.sessions.visibility: "self"`, so session tools can't read another
  person's DM transcript.
- No shell or file tools for this agent on the gateway host: commands there
  inherit the gateway's environment, which holds the bot's token, and a local
  `gbrain` or database URL reads every page.
- Leave the `gbrain-context-engine` slot unset for this bot. It reads through
  the host's own brain connection, not the bot's token.

content.text:
gbrain setup <harness> — give an agent harness memory in one command

Usage: gbrain setup claude-code [flags]
       gbrain setup codex [flags]
       gbrain setup hermes [flags]   (registers MCP through hermes mcp add, then the rule and hook)
       gbrain setup openclaw|opencode|cursor [flags]   (after the harness's own
         MCP registration: writes the brain-first rule and per-turn hook; without it
         agents in a new session seldom call gbrain)

Resolves the brain, source, transport, launcher and registration owner first and
prints them; refuses before writing anything when another owner holds the target.
With no brain configured it creates a keyless local one (gbrain init --pglite
--no-embedding). It then writes the MCP entry and hooks into the harness's own
config and verifies them with the harness_wiring smoke. Codex: [mcp_servers.<name>]
and the hook trust entries in $CODEX_HOME/config.toml, the hooks in hooks.json.

Flags:
  --dry-run            Print the target and every step; write nothing.
  --json               One JSON document on stdout (target, decisions, steps, states).
  --surface S          MCP tool surface: verbs, starter or full, listed in full (default:
                       GBRAIN_SURFACE, then the surface already registered, then starter
                       with only the memory verbs and request_tools listed:
                       serve --surface starter --advertise verbs; full is the opt-in for
                       every operation).
  --scope user|project Wiring scope: every Claude Code session (user, default) or only
                       sessions in this directory (project: ~/.claude.json projects
                       entry + .claude/settings.local.json). Codex: user only.
  --no-hooks           Register MCP only; install no hooks (GBRAIN_HOOKS=0 does the same).
  --capture            Accept automatic capture: also install the capture hooks
                       (Claude Code: Stop and SessionEnd; Codex: SessionEnd).
  --no-capture         Decline automatic capture (the default).
  --providers          Accept provider use: a new brain is created with embeddings.
  --no-providers       Decline provider use (the default: keyless, no paid calls).
  --name NAME          MCP server name (default gbrain); one name per install.
  --source ID          Pin the source the MCP server and hooks use.
  --gbrain-bin PATH    Absolute gbrain launcher (default: the gbrain on PATH).
  --serves one|several Whom the brain serves (default one: nothing changes). several labels each
                       person: config access.serves = several, a member, a folder rule
                       people/<member>/ only that member reads and one key bound to that member
                       (a 0600 file under <config>/member-keys/), then one bound read per member
                       proves it. A one-person setup on a brain that already serves several
                       people (2+ enabled members) refuses rather than write a connection bound
                       to nobody, unless this harness's entry or config mcp.stdio_member binds it.
  --members IDS        The people of --serves several, comma-separated (e.g. alice-example,bob-example).
  --labelled-only      With --serves several: each member's key reads only pages labelled for
                       that member (readable_by or a rule), never the owner's. Opt-in.
  --open-history       With --serves several on a brain that serves one person and already holds
                       pages: let the members read them. Without it or --labelled-only, setup
                       refuses (setup_history_choice_required) and writes nothing.
  --members-file PATH  The same, one id per line.
  --owner ID           With --serves several: the brain owner, added as a member and named with
                       gbrain access owner set when the brain has none (default: your login name
                       as a member id). An existing owner is kept. No key is rebound: setup lists
                       the keys bound to no member with the auth rescope command for each.
  --stdio-member ID    claude-code or codex: write serve --stdio-member ID into this harness's
                       MCP entry, so only its sessions read as ID (an enabled member, or one
                       of --members). Other harnesses on this host are unchanged. Use it for a
                       harness only ID uses; refused where OpenClaw or Hermes is installed
                       (give each person their own HTTP key there). A re-run keeps the entry's
                       member. With --serves several and --shape company or both, an entry
                       with no member is tied to the brain owner.
  --no-stdio-member    Remove --stdio-member from this harness's entry, or leave it unbound.

  --remove             Remove exactly what setup wrote (unchanged entries only), the
                       brain-first instruction block included. The brain and your
                       notes stay. Combine with --dry-run to preview.
  --no-instructions    Opt out of the brain-first instruction block (see below); an
                       existing block is removed and the opt-out is remembered.
                       GBRAIN_AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS=0 does the same.
  --instructions       Opt back in after an earlier --no-instructions.
  --instructions-only  Manage only the brain-first block (on OpenClaw and Hermes, with
                       its per-turn hook): no brain, MCP or other hook changes.
                       Works for a hosted connection too, and for any harness below.
  --workspace DIR      OpenClaw: the agent workspace whose AGENTS.md gets the block
                       (default: agents.defaults.workspace, then ~/.openclaw/workspace).
  --skill-loading M    off (default), spring or resolve. spring adds a compact index of
                       gbrain's bundled skills beside the brain-first block (about
                       1.5k tokens) and loads a skill's full text only when a task
                       matches (gbrain bundled-skill <name>, from this gbrain).
                       resolve (claude-code, codex, hermes) indexes the harness's own
                       skills (~/.claude/skills; Codex: ~/.agents/skills,
                       CODEX_HOME/skills; Hermes: $HERMES_HOME/skills) and adds a
                       separate per-turn hook that names the few skills that fit
                       each prompt (word match; nothing leaves the machine).
                       gbrain setup pi --skill-loading resolve does the same for
                       Pi with an extension in $PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR/extensions.
                       gbrain setup cursor --skill-loading resolve, run in a project,
                       gives Cursor that project's pinned skills only (gbrain skills
                       pin) in .cursor/rules/gbrain-pinned-skills.mdc, kept out of
                       commits; Cursor has no per-turn hook gbrain can use.
                       off removes what an earlier run wrote. The
                       choice is remembered; GBRAIN_SKILL_LOADING sets it too.
  --wakeshift          OpenClaw: install Wakeshift's OpenClaw plugin (@wakeshift/openclaw, pinned)
                       so gbrain can wake an OpenClaw session when a job finishes. Asks
                       consent (--yes), runs OpenClaw's own installer, changes nothing else.
  --shape personal     claude-code, codex: give the brain a personal shape. Writes three
                       empty starter pages, create-only (me/facts, me/voice,
                       me/how-i-decide, each marked status: stub; nothing about you is
                       invented) and a short block beside the brain-first block that
                       tells the agent to read them. A brand-new brain set up without
                       --shape asks (at a terminal) or returns the brain_shape decision
                       (agents); nothing is written until it is answered.
  --shape company      Adds a company source (in default search only when the brain
                       serves one person) with empty pages for company facts,
                       decisions, pricing, customers, calls and playbooks, and the
                       matching lines in that block. --shape both does personal too.
  --shape none         Remove that block; the pages stay.
  --notes DIR          With --shape personal or both: import a notes folder (absolute or
                       ~/), read only, then check keyless search finds a note in it. Over
                       500 markdown files, setup prints the import command instead.
  --docs DIR           With --shape company or both: import a company docs folder into
                       the company source the same way, read only.
  --transcripts DIR    With --shape company or both (not --team): import exported call

gbrain stays current the way gstack does: it rides invocation frequency. A
throttled, cache-read-only check runs at the start of every `gbrain` invocation
(CLI and MCP) and emits an `UPGRADE_AVAILABLE <old> <new>` marker on stderr,
once per 30 minutes per version under one GBRAIN_HOME (a newer version shows at
once). It is one line: when stderr is an interactive TTY a human sees only the
plain `gbrain X -> Y available` sentence instead of the machine token; set
`GBRAIN_FORCE_UPGRADE_MARKER=1` if an agent harness parses the token but runs
under a PTY. `<old>` is always the RUNNING binary's version, so a stale or
foreign-written cache never nags about an upgrade this binary already has. No
host cron required — every agent kind (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes, the
`gbrain serve` host behind a Perplexity thin client) converges to current by
construction. The behavior is governed by one file-plane config key,
`self_upgrade.mode`:

| Mode | Behavior | Who it's for |
|------|----------|--------------|
| `notify` (default) | Emit the marker + a 4-option prompt; never apply without confirmation. | Interactive installs / anyone with a human in the loop. |
| `auto` (opt-in) | Apply silently, but ONLY during quiet hours, ONLY when the brain is idle, doctor-gated, never re-trying a known-bad version, and never installing a release the host's Bun cannot start ([Bun floor](#bun-floor)). | Headless / always-on installs (autopilot daemon, the `gbrain serve` host). |
| `off` | Never check. | Air-gapped / pinned installs. |

Enable hands-off upgrades on an always-on install with one line:

```bash
gbrain config set self_upgrade.mode auto
```

`auto` is deliberately NOT a default anywhere — it's an explicit autonomy grant,
because applying code from GitHub unattended is, by design, remote code

details.aggregated:
gbrain stays current the way gstack does: it rides invocation frequency. A
throttled, cache-read-only check runs at the start of every `gbrain` invocation
(CLI and MCP) and emits an `UPGRADE_AVAILABLE <old> <new>` marker on stderr,
once per 30 minutes per version under one GBRAIN_HOME (a newer version shows at
once). It is one line: when stderr is an interactive TTY a human sees only the
plain `gbrain X -> Y available` sentence instead of the machine token; set
`GBRAIN_FORCE_UPGRADE_MARKER=1` if an agent harness parses the token but runs
under a PTY. `<old>` is always the RUNNING binary's version, so a stale or
foreign-written cache never nags about an upgrade this binary already has. No
host cron required — every agent kind (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes, the
`gbrain serve` host behind a Perplexity thin client) converges to current by
construction. The behavior is governed by one file-plane config key,
`self_upgrade.mode`:

| Mode | Behavior | Who it's for |
|------|----------|--------------|
| `notify` (default) | Emit the marker + a 4-option prompt; never apply without confirmation. | Interactive installs / anyone with a human in the loop. |
| `auto` (opt-in) | Apply silently, but ONLY during quiet hours, ONLY when the brain is idle, doctor-gated, never re-trying a known-bad version, and never installing a release the host's Bun cannot start ([Bun floor](#bun-floor)). | Headless / always-on installs (autopilot daemon, the `gbrain serve` host). |
| `off` | Never check. | Air-gapped / pinned installs. |

Enable hands-off upgrades on an always-on install with one line:

```bash
gbrain config set self_upgrade.mode auto
```
